articleTitle: The infrastructure owners requirements
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Railway Condition Monitoring, 2005 (Ref. No. 2005/10813)
abstract: The purpose of the talk is to give the audience an insight into the infrastructure owners perception of RCM to date. It is also intended to give an understanding of the different customers and their needs and challenges within the infrastructure owners organisation. Finally it endeavours to encourage the wider community involved in the research and development of RCM systems, to meet those needs and challenges.

articleTitle: Condition monitoring of railway signalling - does it have a future and can the signalling supplier help?
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Railway Condition Monitoring, 2005 (Ref. No. 2005/10813)
abstract: A railway signalling company's main role is to design and supply signalling systems and products. However in-service operation is crucial to the smooth running of the railway, and suppliers have to be equally aware of the needs of maintenance and operational staff. Remote condition monitoring can play a big part in fault prevention and maintenance efficiency: signalling suppliers can contribute, not only by incorporating sensible RCM outputs in their equipment, but in providing properly integrated information on the signalled railway to the people who need it.

articleTitle: Current & voltage measuring for railway asset monitoring
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Railway Condition Monitoring, 2005 (Ref. No. 2005/10813)
abstract: Our presentation is based on the experience we have gained throughout the industry on acquiring the measurement and feeding it back to the monitoring system. This is broken into the following segments: (1) introduction - why measure electrical parameters (current and voltage); (2) the development of the technology and overcoming the challenges of the trackside environment; (3) examples of applications and the results achieved.

articleTitle: Fault detection techniques for effective line side asset monitoring
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Railway Condition Monitoring, 2005 (Ref. No. 2005/10813)
abstract: In this paper the results of current research into the state-of-the-art in predictive fault detection and diagnosis methods for railway line-side assets is presented. Research to date has mainly focussed on point machines, track circuits and level crossing systems. It will be argued that, through the use of examples, that the most appropriate method for robust fault detection is based around generic models that are tuned for a particular instance of an asset. Furthermore, once a fault has been detected, it is necessary to have an a priori knowledge of the symptoms that are observable under fault conditions to reliably diagnose faults.

articleTitle: Remote condition monitoring points the maintainers point of view
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Railway Condition Monitoring, 2005 (Ref. No. 2005/10813)
abstract: It is a common myth that remote condition monitoring (RCM) will prevent failures. In the real world it is people such as the maintainer, the installer and the designer actually prevent failures and the biggest burden falls on the maintainer. The principal purpose of RCM is to provide information that will allow the maintainer to act in such a way as to prevent failures. By acting in a timely manner and with good information the maintainer can save the considerable costs of delays caused by failures and additionally reduce the incident risks to both maintenance operatives and to passengers. An RCM system is an asset in its own right that will require maintenance. Such maintenance comes at a cost both in financial and in risk terms, as operatives will be required to go trackside to inspect and repair it. While the maintenance of points and other signalling assets are well within the training and experience of the maintenance operatives, RCM is not, and so this will either have to be sub-contacted out (increasing cost and the likely down time) or significant training of in-house staff will be required. Maintainers are busy people, who anyway make regular visits to their assets, and who by good training and local knowledge, are able to prevent many failures without the need of any RCM system. The challenge for points RCM is to convince the maintainer that RCM will save more money than it costs. Recent high profile failures of RCM Assets have lead many maintainers to be rightly skeptical of the cost benefit of points RCM. It is now up to the points RCM suppliers to show how such systems can be made to work for the maintainer.

articleTitle: What is required from condition monitoring?
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Railway Condition Monitoring, 2005 (Ref. No. 2005/10813)
abstract: The key points of this presentation are: we must not assume condition monitoring is always the 'right' answer; the 'right' answer requires determination of the best appropriate practice on an asset-by-asset basis (PAS55); business case evaluation helps determines the mix of condition monitoring and inspection that is cost effective; in this way we can determine precisely what we want from condition monitoring; and this forms the basis for developing a benefit driven requirement specification.

articleTitle: Overview of techniques
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Railway Condition Monitoring, 2005 (Ref. No. 2005/10813)
abstract: The article provides an overview of the techniques that can be used for condition monitoring of railway equipment, using as an illustrative example a points validation system. Aspects to be covered include fault analysis, fault coverage, sensor selection, signal processing, fault modelling, and communications.

articleTitle: Web services for integrated remote condition monitoring
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Railway Condition Monitoring, 2005 (Ref. No. 2005/10813)
abstract: This paper outlines the motivation for the use of semantic Web-enabled Web services (SWWS) technology for integrated remote condition monitoring of railway infrastructure and train operations. We demonstrate a typical implementation of a proof of concept system, in the form of an RCM Web portal, for predictive maintenance of railway signalling assets.

articleTitle: Point, track circuit and level crossing condition monitoring
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Railway Condition Monitoring, 2005 (Ref. No. 2005/10813)
abstract: Point and track circuit failures are the two most common causes of train delays due to the rail infrastructure and condition monitoring systems designed to detect failures before they occur provide an immediate cost benefit. This talk covers recent progress in the design of such systems, in particular the non invasive monitoring of audio frequency track circuits. Level crossing monitoring provides crucial recorded evidence at this difficult interface between public highway and railway.

articleTitle: Remote condition monitoring - an asset management viewpoint
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Railway Condition Monitoring, 2005 (Ref. No. 2005/10813)
abstract: The presentation considers railway condition monitoring from an asset management viewpoint. The authors explore the importance of asset knowledge and the role of condition monitoring in contributing to this. Expectations and issues associated with railway condition monitoring are considered as part of an asset management strategy.

articleTitle: Posso - Preventief onderhouds- en storingsmeldingssysteem strukton (strukton preventive maintenance and failure diagnosis system)
publicationTitle: IEE Seminar on Railway Condition Monitoring, 2005 (Ref. No. 2005/10813)
abstract: Rail infra monitoring was introduced in the Netherlands by Strukton Railinfra in 1999 under the trademark of POSSreg. Since 2005 a total of 1200 points are monitored nationwide and a decrease of point failures of 60% can be reached. Switch heating monitoring and axle counter monitoring are also in operation. Test sites for level crossings, train detection and axle weight are success full. In Europe POSSreg is in use at sites in Germany, Sweden and Italy.
